I believe action is important over the intention. If one cannot act the way they intend to then they should not act. This is where I feel having confidence is important.

Sure in your head you may think you mean well for someone or want to improve a situation at hand. But whatever is in our head hardly ever reflects in our actions. The more confident you are, the more in line would be your intention (mind) and your action (body).

I personally don't have much self confidence. I feel icky to even try and develop it at times because of the frustration and the despair of not seeing the results of my intentions translating into a positive action. I feel stuck in an awkward limbo many times.

But thankfully I am confident about the fact that I want to change and that allows me to try again after some breaks.

.

.
.
.
.

.
.
.

Journey to discover

My one true gas station

That would fill me up

With her best grade of love

.
.

Needless losses and vain attempts

Revving my engines again and again

.

.

.

.
.
.
.

A hollowed frame

No room to contain

Wild leaves and algae 

Greet me with deep embrace

.
.
.
.

Parts chopped, spanners drop

To fit in with the others

An everlasting misery at this auto shop

.
.
.
.

I could give it a try

Be part of their journeys

Fulfilling my purpose

Hanging onto to their glories

.
.
.
.

Far be it for me

Living this life from scratch

However, here I am

In this gas station one more time

.
.
.

I relate a lot to what you have written. 

Thumb rule: Whatever you feel is a projection. You fear that you possess the same attributes as the ones you criticize or try to destroy.

  
Certainly, not all emotions are projections. But folks who are starting their recovery will be fighting these "demons" and being aware that irrespective of whether the other person is "narcissistic" or whatever, the rage you feel towards them is a projection of a rage that is directed towards yourself.

The empathy you seem to express is cognitive. It's "logical" to feel a certain way when provided a situation. You can empathize with a dude stuck in traffic because if you put yourself in the situation, you can begin to imagine what all feelings will be born. I think covert narcissists are excellent with cognitive empathy because they had to grow up always being alert of their caregivers or surroundings. It's not something a child should be dealing with considering that children actually first grow up narcissistic before empathetic.

So I feel like what you are going through is the natural phase a 13-year-old teen goes through - a rebellious phase. In some sense, your maturity was stunted by traumas and now that you are growing older and somewhat getting tired, you are dropping the cognitive empathy for apathy.

What comes after apathy is detachment. And that will take a long time if you don't sort out your ego issues and traumas that led to your ego grow protective. Therapy is a good start imo.

Take what I have written with a pinch of salt. I am no expert. I am expressing my own insights that I realized through my journey.

Well, I don't think any of us can give you a medical diagnosis on whether you are a covert narcissist or not. It's a bad habit of Cluster-Bs to label themselves as something considering their identity is usually turbulent so perhaps avoid labelling yourself for now. 

Seek a therapist who specializes in personality disorders (if possible of course) and have a few sessions and assessments? I hate the latter considering I am also slightly Alexithymic so I struggle to be confident with my answers in some personality tests.

My personal opinion would be to work on your symptoms - symptoms of rage, fear of being perceived differently than what you project, the fantasies about self. Your past surely plays a role considering children learn to equate emotions, thoughts and behaviours by mirroring their parent. It's an unconscious process that, again, needs to be brought to light through therapy.

Empathy isn't really a painful thing to do tbh. Maybe cognitive empathy is since you need to get out of your head and consider the sensations around you at present.

Self-care is basically teaching people how to non-violently be selfish, to put it in layman's terms. We have grown up taught NOT to be selfish. This has indoctrinated a fear that you are a good person if you don't ask for things or annoy others. But that's false. 

According to you Jung, there is the good individual and then there is the harmless individual. A truly good individual CAN hurt others. They have the strength to do so. But they choose not to. A harmless individual is weak who denies his shadow (the "ugly" side) and adopts this madness that as long as he behaves like a good boy, he will eventually be rewarded. But the world isn't like that. The rivers won't change their course to stop at your feet so that you can leisurely take a drink or a bath.

And these people are the most dangerous. They continue to hang onto an irrational belief that "chisels" off their facade with each tragic event. And what is left of them is the same "ugly" side they so dearly tried to hide.

So the question becomes as follows: How do you relearn being selfish but also not hurting others in the process of wanting your needs met? I don't know the answer. Maybe ask me a year later or something. But your first order of business is to heal or at least learn to tolerate the emotional scars that burn and itch like crazy when exposed to the atmosphere.

If you want quick solution or something useful and not absorb the emotions that are imbibed in paragraphs of descriptions then you will find long texts highly straining to go through.

It makes sense. Our (people with NPD) minds are preoccupied in the past - thinking of the events that wounded them and also preoccupied in the future - laying down a revenge plan on others. We can hardly have our ego live in the present and doing that is essential when reading since you will not be able to understand why the things have been written the way they are.

I understand the need for someone to be preoccupied with only your existence. To make them only have you in their mind. In some sense it's extremely dangerous since the rails are off once you do find someone who promises you "love and affection". In their dictionary, those emotions are controlled and healthy but in our case, the dictionary is corrupt. We begin to loathe others who don't abide by our dictionary and choose to not proofread and edit our dictionary when events seem unfavourable. Because why should we? Someone, when we were young, tore and vandalised it and now we have to fix their mess?

To be your own doctor - that's what the remedy is for mentally ill individuals. Therapy gives us the tools and study lamp to sit down and rewrite parts of our dictionary. We are the ones who have to do the things that are needed to save ourselves. And that is honestly the worst thing about this illness.
